summaryEn: Taiwan's largest pure-play semiconductor test house — the company chips are proven on before they ship. Margins are rising as AI and high-performance testing displaces commodity work, funded by selling its entire Chinese operation and redirecting the proceeds into advanced equipment at home.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + press; test-house framing — the pure-play position, rising gross margin, AI/HPC mix and the China exit funding domestic capex credited, but the disposal gain identified as the source of the 2025Q1 anomaly, capital intensity and customer concentration stated plainly; a CONFLICT between the FinMind FY2025 dividend and the company's announced dividend plan is disclosed rather than resolved; sector/nameZh/years fixed)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
King Yuan Electronics (京元電子, TWSE: 2449) is **Taiwan's largest pure-play semiconductor test house** — the company that proves chips work before they are shipped. It occupies a layer this collection had not covered: ASE, also here, provides packaging **and** test; KYEC does **testing only**, at scale, for phone processors, memory, sensors, automotive chips and, increasingly, **AI silicon**. Founded on **28 May 1987** and **listed in May 2001**, it performs both **wafer-level test** (probing dies before they are cut) and **final test** (verifying packaged parts).

Testing is the semiconductor industry's quality gate, and it has become materially more valuable. Advanced chips take **longer to test**, require **more expensive testers**, and — for AI accelerators and high-performance processors — demand equipment and expertise that few companies possess. The mix shift shows in the margins: **gross margin has climbed steadily from 33.5% (2025Q1) to 39.7% (2026Q1)**, with operating margin rising from 20.8% to **27.2%**. Annual EPS ran **NT$5.59 (FY2022) → 4.78 → 6.37 (FY2024) → NT$9.01 (FY2025)**, and monthly revenue is growing around **29% year-on-year**. Return on equity is **16.6%**.

The most consequential recent decision was **geographic**. KYEC **sold its entire stake in its Chinese subsidiary**, booking a **disposal gain of NT$3.827bn (an earnings contribution of roughly NT$3.13 per share)** — which explains the striking anomaly in its accounts, where **2025Q1 showed a 59.2% net margin against a 20.8% operating margin**. The proceeds were redirected into **advanced test equipment in Taiwan**, with the capital-expenditure budget **raised from NT$7bn to NT$12.28bn**. In effect, the company converted a Chinese asset into domestic AI-testing capacity.

One caution on the data: **FinMind records a FY2025 dividend of NT$1.0 against NT$4.0 for FY2024**, while the company's disposal plan was reported to **add NT$1.5 to dividends in both 2025 and 2026**. These cannot both be complete, so **no claim of a dividend cut is made here** — the discrepancy is flagged for readers to resolve against company filings. The honest read: **a well-positioned pure-play test house with genuinely improving margins, funding an AI-driven capacity build by exiting China — capital-intensive, customer-concentrated, and priced at 32× earnings.**

KYEC was founded in **1987**, in the early years of Taiwan's semiconductor industry, to do the part of chipmaking that almost nobody outside the industry thinks about: **testing**. Every chip must be verified — probed at the wafer stage to identify which dies are good, and tested again after packaging to confirm the finished part meets specification across voltage, temperature and speed. Chips that fail are discarded; chips that pass are sorted into performance grades.

The business model is unglamorous and capital-intensive. Test houses buy **very expensive automated test equipment**, then sell **time on it**. Profitability depends on **utilisation, test-time efficiency and the mix of chips being tested** — a simple sensor takes seconds, a complex processor takes far longer and requires far more sophisticated equipment. The company **listed in May 2001**, and built itself into **Taiwan's largest independent test provider**, deliberately remaining a **pure-play** rather than following peers into packaging.

Two forces have reshaped it recently. The first is **AI and high-performance computing**: advanced processors and accelerators need **longer test times on more expensive testers**, which raises revenue per chip and favours the operators with the newest equipment and the deepest expertise. The second is **geopolitics**. KYEC **sold its entire Chinese subsidiary**, realising a gain of **NT$3.827bn**, and redirected the money into **advanced test capacity in Taiwan** — raising planned capital spending from **NT$7bn to NT$12.28bn**. That was both a de-risking of its China exposure and a bet that the highest-value testing work will be done at home, close to the foundries and designers driving the AI cycle.

- **1987 (28 May)** — King Yuan Electronics founded to provide semiconductor **wafer and final test** services.
- **1990s** — Grows with Taiwan's semiconductor industry as a **pure-play test house**, deliberately not entering packaging.
- **2001 (9 May)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (2449)**.
- **2000s–2010s** — Becomes **Taiwan's largest independent test provider**, serving phone processors, memory, sensors and automotive chips; establishes a Chinese subsidiary.
- **2022** — EPS **NT$5.59**; dividend NT$3.5.
- **2023** — Cyclical dip: EPS **NT$4.78**; dividend NT$3.2.
- **2024** — Recovery: EPS **NT$6.37**; dividend **NT$4.0**.
- **2025** — **Sells its entire Chinese subsidiary** for a **disposal gain of NT$3.827bn (~NT$3.13 per share)**; raises capital spending from **NT$7bn to NT$12.28bn** for advanced test equipment in Taiwan. **EPS NT$9.01**; gross margin climbs from 33.5% to 37.7% through the year.
- **2026Q1** — **Gross margin 39.7%, operating margin 27.2%**; EPS NT$1.87; monthly revenue growing around **29% year-on-year**.

KYEC's accounts show a **capital-intensive service business improving its mix**, plus one very large one-off.

- **Margins rising steadily — the most important trend.** **Gross margin climbed from 33.5% (2025Q1) to 39.7% (2026Q1)**, and operating margin from **20.8% to 27.2%**. For a test house, this reflects **mix**: AI and high-performance chips require longer test times on more advanced equipment, raising revenue per unit of capacity.
- **The 2025Q1 anomaly, explained.** That quarter showed a **59.2% net margin against a 20.8% operating margin** — a gap of nearly 40 points. The cause is the **sale of the entire Chinese subsidiary**, which produced a **disposal gain of NT$3.827bn (roughly NT$3.13 per share)**. This is a **non-recurring item**, and FY2025's headline EPS of **NT$9.01** should be read with that in mind: the **operating margin, not the net margin, describes the ongoing business**.
- **Capital intensity is the model.** **NT$113.2bn of assets** against **NT$54.4bn of equity** and a **51.9% debt ratio**, with **NT$14.4bn of cash**. Test equipment is expensive and depreciates; **operating cash flow of NT$3.74bn** in 2026Q1 comfortably exceeded **NT$2.29bn of net income**, the usual pattern for an equipment-heavy business.
- **Capital spending sharply raised.** From **NT$7bn to NT$12.28bn**, funded partly by the China disposal, and directed at **advanced test capacity in Taiwan**.
- **A dividend record with an unresolved discrepancy.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year) rose steadily: **NT$1.35 (2018) → 1.8 → 2.0 → 3.0 → 3.5 (2022) → 3.2 (2023) → NT$4.0 (2024)**. For **FY2025 FinMind records NT$1.0**, while the company's disposal plan was reported to **add NT$1.5 to dividends in 2025 and 2026** on top of a base expectation. **These figures are inconsistent**, so this page does not assert a dividend cut; readers should verify the FY2025 distribution against company filings.
- **Valuation.** **P/E 32.0×**, **P/B 5.30×**, yield **0.64%**.

The financing reality: **an improving, capital-hungry test franchise that funded its next phase by selling its Chinese business** — with one large non-recurring gain in the record and one dividend figure that does not reconcile.

**Stance: Taiwan's largest pure-play test house, with genuinely improving margins as AI testing displaces commodity work — funded by exiting China, and priced at 32x for a capital-intensive service business.**

The bull case:

1. **A necessary layer with improving economics.** Every chip must be tested, and **advanced chips take longer on more expensive equipment**. That mix shift is visible: **gross margin up from 33.5% to 39.7%**, operating margin from **20.8% to 27.2%** — the clearest evidence that AI and high-performance work is displacing commodity testing.
2. **A decisive capital reallocation.** Selling the **entire Chinese subsidiary** for a **NT$3.827bn gain** and redirecting proceeds into Taiwanese advanced test capacity — with capex raised from **NT$7bn to NT$12.28bn** — removes geopolitical exposure and concentrates investment where the AI cycle is.
3. **Scale and position.** Taiwan's largest independent test provider, with **monthly revenue growing ~29%**, **ROE 16.6%** and operating cash flow comfortably above net income.

The counter-arguments:

- **Capital intensity caps returns.** Test equipment is expensive, depreciates and must be continually replaced. **ROE of 16.6%** is respectable but far below the fabless and IP businesses elsewhere in this collection — and the capex increase to NT$12.28bn will weigh before it pays.
- **The FY2025 headline flatters.** **EPS of NT$9.01 includes a ~NT$3.13 disposal gain.** The recurring earnings base is materially lower, which matters when assessing a 32× multiple.
- **Customer and cycle concentration.** Test demand follows chip volumes and the same hyperscaler capital spending that drives much of this collection; a downturn leaves expensive equipment idle.
- **An unresolved dividend discrepancy** between recorded and announced figures.

A **mix-improvement** thesis: a solid, necessary business genuinely moving up the value chain — provided one values it on recurring, not reported, earnings.

KYEC sells **time on very expensive machines**, and its economics follow directly from that:

- **Wafer test (probe).** Before a wafer is cut into individual dies, each die is probed to determine whether it works. This identifies yield and prevents good money being spent packaging bad chips.
- **Final test.** After packaging, the finished chip is tested again — across **voltage, temperature and frequency** — to confirm it meets specification and to sort parts into performance grades (which directly determines what the chipmaker can charge for them).
- **How revenue and profit arise.** Customers pay for **test time**. Profitability is driven by three things: **utilisation** (idle testers are pure loss), **test-time efficiency** (engineering that shortens the test without compromising coverage), and **mix** (a complex AI accelerator occupies advanced equipment far longer than a simple sensor, at a much higher rate).
- **Why AI improves the economics.** High-performance processors and accelerators require **longer test times on newer, costlier equipment** — exactly the work that raises revenue per machine-hour. This is why **gross margin rose from 33.5% to 39.7%** without any change in the underlying business model.
- **The capital cycle.** Advanced testers must be bought ahead of demand, which is why capex was **raised from NT$7bn to NT$12.28bn** and why the **China disposal proceeds** were redirected into domestic equipment.

The levers are **utilisation, chip mix (AI/HPC versus commodity), test-time engineering, and capital-expenditure timing**. The strength is that testing is **non-optional and increasingly demanding**, and that a pure-play with scale can invest in the newest equipment across many customers. The vulnerability is structural: **fixed, depreciating assets meeting cyclical demand** — when chip volumes fall, testers sit idle and depreciation continues regardless.

Semiconductor testing is a **necessary, capital-intensive service layer** that has quietly become more valuable.

- **Where it sits.** After fabrication (TSMC, UMC) and alongside packaging (ASE), testing verifies that chips work. Some chipmakers test in-house; many outsource to specialists, either to packaging-and-test houses (**OSATs** like ASE) or to **pure-play test companies** like KYEC. The pure-play model trades breadth for focus: all capital goes into test equipment and test engineering.
- **Why the layer is gaining value.** Advanced chips are **harder and slower to test**. More transistors mean more possible faults; higher speeds require more sophisticated equipment; AI accelerators and HPC processors demand **long test times on the most expensive testers**. Test cost as a share of total chip cost has been rising — which is exactly what KYEC's expanding margins reflect.
- **The competitive set.** KYEC competes with OSATs' test operations (ASE, Amkor), other Taiwanese test houses, and customers' in-house capacity. Competition turns on **equipment fleet, engineering capability, capacity availability and price** — and on being qualified with the chip designers whose parts must be tested.
- **The geopolitical dimension.** Test capacity, like fabrication, has become politically sensitive. KYEC's decision to **exit China entirely** and concentrate investment in Taiwan reflects a broader realignment in which supply-chain location matters to customers as much as capability.

KYEC's position is **strong within its layer**: Taiwan's largest independent test house, investing heavily in advanced capacity as AI raises the technical bar. The industry truth is that **testing is indispensable but capital-hungry** — it captures a modest, reliable slice of every chip made, and its returns are set by how well a company matches expensive equipment to demand that it does not control.

**Strengths**
- **Taiwan's largest pure-play test house**, with both wafer and final test at scale across phone, memory, sensor, automotive and AI chips.
- **Improving mix and margins**: gross **33.5% → 39.7%**, operating **20.8% → 27.2%**; EPS **NT$5.59 → 9.01**; revenue **+29% YoY**.
- **Decisive capital reallocation**: entire China subsidiary sold for a **NT$3.827bn gain**, capex raised **NT$7bn → NT$12.28bn** for advanced Taiwanese capacity.

**Weaknesses**
- **Capital-intensive** with heavy depreciation; **ROE 16.6%** modest versus asset-light peers.
- **FY2025 EPS of NT$9.01 includes a ~NT$3.13 non-recurring disposal gain**.
- **Dividend data conflict** for FY2025 (recorded NT$1.0 versus an announced plan to add NT$1.5).

**Opportunities**
- **AI and HPC testing** requiring longer test times on advanced equipment — higher revenue per machine-hour.
- Supply-chain realignment favouring Taiwan-based test capacity.
- Test-time engineering improving throughput on existing assets.

**Threats**
- **Chip-volume downturn** leaving expensive testers idle while depreciation continues.
- Competition from OSAT test operations and in-house capacity.
- Capex timing risk — advanced testers bought ahead of demand that may not arrive on schedule.

- **Reported FY2025 earnings are inflated by a one-off.** **EPS of NT$9.01 includes roughly NT$3.13 from the China disposal gain (NT$3.827bn)**. The recurring earnings base is materially lower, and a **32× multiple applied to the headline figure overstates the valuation support**. Use the operating margin, not the net margin, to judge the business.
- **Capital intensity and cyclicality combined.** Advanced testers are expensive, must be bought ahead of demand, and depreciate whether or not they run. With capex raised to **NT$12.28bn**, a slowdown in chip volumes would leave fixed costs against idle capacity — the classic risk of this business model.
- **Demand is derived, not controlled.** Test volumes follow chip production, which follows end demand and hyperscaler capital spending. KYEC has no influence over any of it.
- **Customer concentration and qualification.** Test work is qualified per device with specific customers; losing a major programme, or a customer bringing testing in-house, would leave dedicated capacity stranded.
- **Competitive pressure.** OSATs (ASE, Amkor) run large test operations and can bundle packaging and test; pure-play focus is an advantage in equipment investment but a disadvantage in bundling.
- **Unresolved dividend information.** Recorded and announced FY2025 dividend figures do not reconcile; investors should confirm the actual distribution from company filings rather than rely on either source.

KYEC's outlook turns on whether the **mix shift toward AI testing continues to lift margins faster than capital spending weighs on returns.** The axes to watch:

- **Gross and operating margin.** The single clearest indicator, and currently the most encouraging: **gross margin up from 33.5% to 39.7%** and operating margin from **20.8% to 27.2%** in four quarters. Continued expansion would confirm that AI and HPC testing is genuinely displacing commodity work.
- **Utilisation of the new capacity.** Capex has been raised to **NT$12.28bn** for advanced test equipment in Taiwan. Whether that equipment is filled — and how quickly — determines whether the China disposal was converted into earnings or into depreciation.
- **Recurring earnings, excluding the disposal.** FY2025's **NT$9.01** included roughly **NT$3.13 of one-off gain**. The base rate of profitability, and its trajectory in 2026, is what should be valued.
- **Chip volumes and AI demand.** Test demand is derived from production; the same hyperscaler capital cycle that drives Wiwynn, King Slide and Elite Material elsewhere in this collection ultimately sets KYEC's volumes too.

Bottom line: KYEC is **Taiwan's largest pure-play semiconductor test house**, occupying a necessary layer whose economics are genuinely improving — **gross margin up from 33.5% to 39.7%** as AI and high-performance chips demand longer tests on costlier equipment — and it has **sold its entire Chinese operation for a NT$3.827bn gain to fund NT$12.28bn of advanced capacity at home**. The honest qualifiers are that **FY2025's NT$9.01 EPS includes about NT$3.13 of that one-off gain**, that the business is **capital-intensive with a 16.6% ROE**, that **demand is entirely derived**, and that its **FY2025 dividend figures do not reconcile across sources**. Judge it on **margin trajectory and utilisation of new capacity** — a solid, necessary business moving up the value chain, valued on earnings that need adjusting first.
